text: Nobody here has reached Vietnam yet, and that gap is where the film does its work. Four recruits share a barracks; what cracks them open is not combat but what one of them turns out to be, and the discovery moves through the room like weather. Robert Altman spends 118 minutes almost entirely inside that confinement, where a sentence said at the wrong moment travels further than it would outdoors. A Grand Jury Prize and a Volpi Cup for acting followed, a strange haul for a picture with no spectacle in it: no jungle, no landing zone, only young men rehearsing a violence they still believe is somewhere else. The prejudice under examination is never announced as a theme. It sits in their mouths, in the jokes, in the small courtesies that keep failing.

A man gets off a bus in a town he does not know and answers to a dead stranger's name. El otro runs 83 minutes, which for a premise this combustible is a decision in itself: Ariel Rotter is not building a thriller out of the switch but watching what a borrowed identity does to a face over a few quiet days. The stakes are not exposure so much as appetite. Once a businessman has tried being nobody in particular, the life waiting for him at home has to be argued for again from the beginning, and the film gives him plenty of quiet in which to postpone the argument. Two Silver Bears came of it, one the jury's grand prize and one for the lead performance, a fair indication of where the camera stays: on one man, doing very little, visibly.

The grievance is one sentence long, and the distance it has to travel is the whole width of a country. Li Xuelian's husband says something about her that is not true, and she sets out from a county town to have it corrected, moving up through offices that each pass her to the next. Feng Xiaogang gives this 128 minutes of patience, because the joke and the injury are one object and neither can be hurried. The comedy needs its imbalance: one stubborn woman, an apparatus with nobody in it to blame, a claim so small that no official can justify the cost of settling it. It took Best Film at the Asian Film Awards and a Golden Shell. What stays is how much of a life a person will spend on a fact everyone else finds too minor to hold.

In a Mennonite settlement in northern Mexico, a married farmer has fallen in love with a woman who is not his wife. Carlos Reygadas takes 136 minutes with this, at a tempo set by fields and milking and the length of a working day, so that a conversation across a kitchen table carries the weight of an event. What stands to be lost is not reputation but the whole scaffolding: a faith, a marriage, children, a community arranged precisely against this. Nothing is smuggled. The film sits on TSPDT's 1,000 Greatest Films, took a Jury Prize and an Ariel for best picture, and went forward as Mexico's submission to the Academy Awards. Its difficulty is to keep one man's tenderness toward two women legible at once, without either becoming the mistake.

The child is found in a cabbage patch, and the city he grows into has no work to give him. Vittorio De Sica spends 97 minutes holding apart two registers nobody else would have put in one film: a fairy tale complete with a kind old woman, and a vacant lot outside post-war Milan where the homeless build themselves a town out of scrap. Totò organizes them, and for a while it functions. Then the land turns out to be worth money to someone else. Italy lists the film among the 100 it means to save; it took a Palme d'Or and holds a place on TSPDT's 1,000 Greatest Films. The comedy is genuine and so is the arithmetic of eviction, and neither is allowed to cancel the other out.

A detective with a gun and a badge is hidden inside a community that wants neither. Peter Weir builds Witness on that friction, and the surprise is how domestic the tension turns out to be: a city man learning how to move, how to speak, how to fail at disappearing among Amish farmers whose child saw a killing. 112 minutes, a good part of it quiet labor and watching. Academy recognition came for acting, cinematography and direction; the Writers Guild named the original screenplay, and the National Board of Review put the film in its ten best of the year. The thriller machinery is honored rather than abandoned, but what holds is smaller: glances across a kitchen, and the standing chance that the people hunting him know where to look.

The pills come first thing in the morning, the show goes on, and the film declines to treat those as two separate stories. Joe Gideon directs and choreographs musical theater at the top of the profession while his private life comes apart on a schedule he seems to have set himself. Bob Fosse cuts 123 minutes to that rhythm, work and damage keeping the same time. What is at stake is not success, already secured, but whether a person can spend himself as fuel and still expect the account to balance. Academy Awards came for acting, cinematography and costume design; a Palme d'Or too, with the National Film Registry and TSPDT's 1,000 Greatest Films after it. Few films about ego are this entertained by their subject and this cold about the bill.

Two people file for divorce and then set about ruining each other's chances with everyone else. The Awful Truth runs 91 minutes on that engine, and the speed is the argument: Leo McCarey lets the sabotage escalate faster than either party can admit what it means. 1937, and the decorum of the period is load-bearing. Everything indecent has to be conducted in drawing rooms, through introductions, in front of people who cannot be seen to notice. Academy Awards arrived for direction, for the lead performance and for editing, which in a film built of interruptions is no minor department. It sits in the National Film Registry and on TSPDT's 1,000 Greatest Films. The premise is malice; the effect, oddly, is tenderness.

The island the army assigns them to has no enemy on it, and before long it has no army either. A handful of Italian soldiers are put ashore in the Greek sea in the middle of a war to watch for ships that never come, and then the vessel that dropped them is sunk. Gabriele Salvatores makes 96 minutes out of that suspension: a comedy whose premise is dereliction, and whose sweetness cannot be separated from the fact that these men are being spared a slaughter their countrymen are not. The village looks abandoned at first. What the island slowly makes of them, and what they begin to want instead of rescue, is the real business. It took the Academy Award for international feature and David di Donatello awards for film and direction. Every peaceful day here is borrowed from somebody else's disaster.

The desert is not the hard part; what comes after leaving the community is. Samson is fifteen and cheeky, Delilah lives in the same isolated place in the Central Australian desert, and Warwick Thornton follows them out into a country with less room in it than the one they left. He keeps the scale small: 101 minutes, two young people, a distance covered mostly on foot and on nothing. Pity and uplift are both declined. Love here is not a reward handed out for suffering, it is the only shelter going, improvised daily by two people nobody is looking for. A Caméra d'Or, the AACTA for best film with acting awards beside it, a place on Australian critics' 2018 list of the century's top twenty-five. The camera waits with them through the hours when nothing is being decided.

A husband brings home a stranger, an elderly Holocaust survivor taken in without discussion, and the marriage has to make room. Giovanna is tired in the way that has no incident attached to it, and Ferzan Özpetek uses the old man as a solvent: a past too large to keep quiet, set down in a household that has stopped telling itself anything. Across the way there is a window, and a man in it. Italian in language and in temperature, British on the paperwork, the film moves between two periods without turning the older one into a lesson for the younger. It won a Crystal Globe and David di Donatello awards for film and direction. The subject in the end is appetite in middle life: what a person has quietly settled for, and how fast that settlement reopens.

Munich, 1943: a student and her brother carry pamphlets into a university building, and she is caught. Most of Marc Rothemund's 117 minutes stay in the room that follows. The drama is procedural in the strictest sense - question, answer, revision, the narrowing of what can still be said - and it rests on two people trying to fix a version of events the other cannot break. The White Rose printed words; the state answered with a process. Silver Bears for direction and for the lead performance point at the same decision: to trust a table, two chairs and a transcript rather than stage the history around them. What holds is the sound of a mind working at speed, under conditions built to make that useless.

A girl dies on her birthday, and her family has settled on the word accident before the night is over. The police and social services want a reason; the household offers them a routine instead. Alexandros Avranas holds the camera at a fixed, well-mannered distance for 99 minutes, framing rooms in a Greek apartment where the furniture is square to the walls and the timetable is observed. The investigation proceeds outside. Inside, the household goes on functioning, which is the harder thing to watch. The withholding is not a puzzle-box trick; it reproduces the position of the caseworker at the door, receiving polite answers. A Silver Lion for direction and a Volpi Cup for acting followed. The discipline is total, and the subject is authority.

Laundry is the work, and the film keeps its eye on what the work costs a woman with no other means. Lantier walks out on Gervaise; she marries a roofer named Coupeau; the household is assembled and then, by degrees, taken apart by drink and by an accident that removes a wage. René Clément films Paris as an economy rather than a backdrop, courtyards and wash-houses and stairwell traffic, where every small reversal carries an exact price. 112 minutes, nearly all of it the labor of staying solvent and respectable at once. The lead performance took a Volpi Cup, a BAFTA followed for its actor, and France sent the film to the Academy Awards. What the picture watches is one woman's ledger, kept honestly, running short.
